items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Muir explains how mountain streams carry away the waste that earlier visitors left behind.
Muir finds the mountain landscape full of life and meaning, with each part connected to the rest.
Muir argues that the mountains are interesting only to people who study them very closely.
Muir describes speaking aloud to the plants and animals as his way of passing long, lonely days.

items.explanation: Muir says nothing in the landscape is dead or dull, that everything is full of lessons, and that anything we try to pick out is “hitched to everything else in the universe.” The text's main idea is this living, connected quality.

rationales.A: Muir says the landscape holds no trace of rubbish or waste, so there is nothing for streams to carry away.
rationales.C: Muir says the interest attaches to everything, not that only close study makes it interesting.
rationales.D: Muir only says “we feel like” speaking to plants and animals, a figure for feeling kinship, not a habit he describes.

passage.intro: The following text is from John Muir's 1911 book My First Summer in the Sierra, a journal of the summer of 1869, which he spent in the Sierra Nevada mountains of California.
passage.text: No Sierra landscape that I have seen holds anything truly dead or dull, or any trace of what in manufactories is called rubbish or waste; everything is perfectly clean and pure and full of divine lessons. This quick, inevitable interest attaching to everything seems marvelous until the hand of God becomes visible; then it seems reasonable that what interests Him may well interest us. When we try to pick out anything by itself, we find it hitched to everything else in the universe. One fancies a heart like our own must be beating in every crystal and cell, and we feel like stopping to speak to the plants and animals as friendly fellow mountaineers.

source.author: John Muir
source.title: My First Summer in the Sierra

items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The narrator's mother insisted on complicated designs and would not let her daughter use simple shapes.
The narrator preferred simple shapes because her mother praised them more than any original design.
The narrator's mother scolded her so often that the narrator became afraid to make choices of her own.
The narrator's quiet, watchful mother made her feel trusted and responsible for her own work.

items.explanation: The narrator says the “quietness of her oversight” made her feel “strongly responsible and dependent upon my own judgment,” and that her mother treated her as “a dignified little individual.” That trust and responsibility is the main idea.

rationales.A: The narrator says she usually drew “easy and simple crosses and squares,” and nothing suggests her mother forbade them.
rationales.B: The text names faults her mother disliked in original designs but never says her mother praised simple shapes more.
rationales.C: A rebuke is mentioned once, and it humiliated the narrator because rebukes were rare, not because they were constant.

passage.intro: The following text is from Zitkala-Ša's 1921 book American Indian Stories. She recalls learning beadwork from her mother as a child.
passage.text: After some experience I usually drew easy and simple crosses and squares. These were some of the set forms. My original designs were not always symmetrical nor sufficiently characteristic, two faults with which my mother had little patience. The quietness of her oversight made me feel strongly responsible and dependent upon my own judgment. She treated me as a dignified little individual as long as I was on my good behavior; and how humiliated I was when some boldness of mine drew forth a rebuke from her!

items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Washington saw an ordinary cleaning task as a chance to prove that he deserved to be admitted.
Washington was annoyed that the head teacher assigned him a chore instead of a real examination.
Washington worried that he did not know how to sweep a room well enough to satisfy the teacher.
Washington believed the head teacher had already decided to admit him before he began sweeping.

items.explanation: Washington calls the order “my chance,” receives it “with more delight” than any order, and feels his “future depended upon the impression” the cleaning made. He treats the chore as a test of his worth.

rationales.B: Washington says he never received an order with more delight, which is the opposite of annoyance.
rationales.C: Nothing in the text expresses doubt about his ability to sweep; he sees the task only as an opportunity.
rationales.D: Washington says his future depended on the impression he made, so he did not think the decision was already made.

passage.intro: The following text is from Booker T. Washington's 1901 autobiography Up from Slavery. As a teenager, he has arrived at a school whose head teacher has not yet decided whether to admit him.
passage.text:
After some hours had passed, the head teacher said to me: “The adjoining recitation-room needs sweeping. Take the broom and sweep it.”

It occurred to me at once that here was my chance. Never did I receive an order with more delight. . . . I had the feeling that in a large measure my future depended upon the impression I made upon the teacher in the cleaning of that room.

items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Worms damage the smooth surface of fields, so the turf must be repaired every few years.
The beauty of a field depends mostly on the kinds of grass that grow in it.
Worms, though easily overlooked, steadily reshape the soil that forms a smooth field.
The soil of a field is replaced every few years by soil carried in from elsewhere.

items.explanation: Darwin says a field's smoothness is “mainly due to” worms levelling it and that all the surface soil passes through worms every few years. The main idea is that unnoticed worms keep reshaping the land's surface.

rationales.A: Darwin credits worms with creating the smoothness, not with damaging it.
rationales.B: Darwin attributes the field's beauty to its smoothness, which worms produce, and does not discuss kinds of grass.
rationales.D: The soil passes through the bodies of worms on the spot; Darwin does not say it is replaced from somewhere else.

passage.intro: The following text is from Charles Darwin's 1881 book The Formation of Vegetable Mould, through the Action of Worms.
passage.text: When we behold a wide, turf-covered expanse, we should remember that its smoothness, on which so much of its beauty depends, is mainly due to all the inequalities having been slowly levelled by worms. It is a marvellous reflection that the whole of the superficial mould over any such expanse has passed, and will again pass, every few years through the bodies of worms.

source.author: Charles Darwin
source.title: The Formation of Vegetable Mould, through the Action of Worms

items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Buck learns about the gold discovery by reading newspapers and decides to travel north.
Steamship companies urge dog owners to send their animals to the Northland to search for gold.
A gold rush in the far north has created a demand for strong dogs, which puts dogs like Buck at risk.
Dogs with long, warm hair suffer in the southern towns where most of them were raised.

items.explanation: Gold found in the Arctic sends thousands of men north, and those men want heavy, strong dogs with warm coats. The text says trouble is “brewing” for every such dog, including Buck.

rationales.A: The text says Buck did not read the newspapers, which is why he does not know trouble is coming.
rationales.B: The companies are “booming the find” to attract men, and nothing says they appeal to dog owners.
rationales.D: The text describes the dogs' warm hair as what makes them wanted in the north, not as a source of suffering.

passage.intro: The following text is from Jack London's 1903 novel The Call of the Wild. Buck is a large dog living on a ranch in California.
passage.text: Buck did not read the newspapers, or he would have known that trouble was brewing, not alone for himself, but for every tide-water dog, strong of muscle and with warm, long hair, from Puget Sound to San Diego. Because men, groping in the Arctic darkness, had found a yellow metal, and because steamship and transportation companies were booming the find, thousands of men were rushing into the Northland. These men wanted dogs, and the dogs they wanted were heavy dogs, with strong muscles by which to toil, and furry coats to protect them from the frost.

items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Miss Taylor was more a close friend than an authority to Emma, so Emma mostly did as she pleased.
Miss Taylor was a strict governess whose rules shaped Emma's habits from an early age.
Emma valued Miss Taylor's judgment so highly that she followed her advice in nearly everything.
Emma and her sister competed for Miss Taylor's attention throughout their childhood.

items.explanation: Miss Taylor was “less as a governess than a friend,” her mildness “hardly allowed her to impose any restraint,” and Emma did “just what she liked.” The main idea is a warm friendship with little authority in it.

rationales.B: The text says Miss Taylor's mildness hardly allowed her to impose any restraint, so she was not strict.
rationales.C: Emma highly esteemed Miss Taylor's judgment, but the text says she was “directed chiefly by her own.”
rationales.D: Miss Taylor was fond of both daughters, and nothing in the text suggests the sisters competed for her.

passage.intro: The following text is from Jane Austen's 1815 novel Emma.
passage.text: Sixteen years had Miss Taylor been in Mr. Woodhouse's family, less as a governess than a friend, very fond of both daughters, but particularly of Emma. Between them it was more the intimacy of sisters. Even before Miss Taylor had ceased to hold the nominal office of governess, the mildness of her temper had hardly allowed her to impose any restraint; and the shadow of authority being now long passed away, they had been living together as friend and friend very mutually attached, and Emma doing just what she liked; highly esteeming Miss Taylor's judgment, but directed chiefly by her own.

items.stem: Based on the text, why does the narrator know so little about Captain Littlepage?

choices.text: The captain has only recently moved to the village.
The narrator has been too busy with her own work to visit him.
Mrs. Todd avoids explaining him, treating him as one of her secrets.
The captain refuses to speak with anyone who is not a sailor.

items.explanation: When the narrator asks about the captain, Mrs. Todd shakes her head and seems “to class him with her other secrets.” The narrator's main source of information will not explain him.

rationales.A: The narrator has seen him “once or twice before,” and the text gives no sign that he is new to the village.
rationales.B: The text describes the narrator asking questions about him, not being too busy to learn more.
rationales.D: Nothing in the text describes the captain refusing to speak to anyone.

passage.intro: The following text is from Sarah Orne Jewett's 1896 novel The Country of the Pointed Firs. The narrator is staying with Mrs. Todd, an herbalist in a small coastal village.
passage.text: This was Captain Littlepage, whom I had seen only once or twice before, sitting pale and old behind a closed window; never out of doors until now. Mrs. Todd always shook her head gravely when I asked a question, and said that he wasn't what he had been once, and seemed to class him with her other secrets. He might have belonged with a simple which grew in a certain slug-haunted corner of the garden, whose use she could never be betrayed into telling me, though I saw her cutting the tops by moonlight once, as if it were a charm, and not a medicine, like the great fading bloodroot leaves.

source.author: Sarah Orne Jewett
source.title: The Country of the Pointed Firs

items.originalText: In his 1854 book Walden, Henry David Thoreau explains why he moved to a small cabin in the woods. He suggests that he wanted to experience life honestly, even if it turned out to be disappointing.
items.stem: Which quotation from Walden most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.text: “I did not wish to live what was not life, living is so dear”
“to cut a broad swath and shave close”
“if it proved to be mean, why then to get the whole and genuine meanness of it”
“nor did I wish to practise resignation, unless it was quite necessary”

items.explanation: “Mean” here means poor or worthless. Thoreau says that if life proved mean, he wanted to know “the whole and genuine meanness of it,” so he would accept a disappointing truth rather than avoid it.

rationales.A: This shows that Thoreau valued real life, but it says nothing about accepting life if it proved disappointing.
rationales.B: This describes living thoroughly, but it does not address what he would do if life turned out to be disappointing.
rationales.D: This says he did not want to give up and accept things, which is not the same as facing a disappointing truth.

items.originalText: In My First Summer in the Sierra (1911), John Muir describes finding a rare lily in the mountains of California. Muir makes clear that he thought the flower was worth suffering real hardship to see.
items.stem: Which quotation from My First Summer in the Sierra most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.text: “A lovely flower, worth going hungry and footsore endless miles to see.”
“Its bulbs are buried in shaggy chaparral tangles, I suppose for safety from pawing bears”
“big, bold, blunt-nosed bees drone and mumble in its polleny bells”
“The whole world seems richer now that I have found this plant in so noble a landscape.”

items.explanation: Going “hungry and footsore endless miles” names real hardship, and Muir says the lily is “worth” it. This quotation states the claim directly.

rationales.B: This explains where the bulbs grow and why, without saying anything about hardship worth enduring.
rationales.C: This describes the bees visiting the flower rather than what the flower is worth to Muir.
rationales.D: This shows how much Muir values the lily, but it does not mention any hardship he would endure.

quoteSource.author: John Muir
quoteSource.title: My First Summer in the Sierra

items.originalText: In Charlotte Perkins Gilman's 1915 novel Herland, the narrator, Vandyck Jennings, joins his friends Terry and Jeff on an expedition. Early in the novel, Jennings reveals that he values any subject mainly for what it shows about people.
items.stem: Which quotation from Herland most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.text: “As for me, sociology's my major. You have to back that up with a lot of other sciences, of course.”
“I'm interested in them all.”
“Terry was strong on facts—geography and meteorology and those”
“I didn't care what it was they talked about, so long as it connected with human life”

items.explanation: The narrator says the topic itself does not matter to him “so long as it connected with human life.” That condition shows he values subjects for what they reveal about people.

rationales.A: Naming his major and the sciences behind it shows what he studies, not why a subject matters to him.
rationales.B: This shows the narrator's broad interests, but not that his interest depends on a subject's connection to people.
rationales.C: This describes Terry's strengths rather than the narrator's own values.

items.originalText: In Charlotte Perkins Gilman's 1892 short story “The Yellow Wallpaper,” the narrator's husband, John, is a doctor who directs her rest cure. Throughout the story, John discourages the narrator from using her imagination.
items.stem: Which quotation from “The Yellow Wallpaper” most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.text: “I always fancy I see people walking in these numerous paths and arbors”
“Out of another I get a lovely view of the bay and a little private wharf belonging to the estate.”
“John has cautioned me not to give way to fancy in the least.”
“So I try.”

items.explanation: “Fancy” means imagination here, and John has “cautioned” her not to give way to it “in the least.” This quotation shows John discouraging her imagination.

rationales.A: This shows the narrator's imagination at work, but it does not show John's response to it.
rationales.B: This describes the view from a window and does not involve John or the narrator's imagination.
rationales.D: This shows the narrator trying to follow advice, but on its own it does not show who gave the advice or what it was.

items.originalText: In Jane Austen's 1815 novel Emma, Emma's governess and close friend, Miss Taylor, marries and moves to a house half a mile away. Austen suggests that Emma's father, though loving, cannot replace the companionship Miss Taylor provided.
items.stem: Which quotation from Emma most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.text: “It was true that her friend was going only half a mile from them”
“She dearly loved her father, but he was no companion for her.”
“with all her advantages, natural and domestic”
“she was now in great danger of suffering from intellectual solitude”

items.explanation: The claim has two parts: the father is loving, and he cannot provide companionship. “She dearly loved her father, but he was no companion for her” states both.

rationales.A: This concerns how far away Miss Taylor will live, not what Emma's father can offer.
rationales.C: This mentions Emma's advantages and says nothing about her father.
rationales.D: This shows Emma will be lonely, but it does not mention her father or his limits as a companion.

items.context: Thoreau listed what he paid for each material. A student claims that boards were the most expensive material Thoreau bought for the house.

table.title: Cost of the materials for Thoreau's house

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the student's claim?

choices.text: The materials for the house cost $28.12½ in all, and the boards cost $8.03½.
The boards cost $8.03½, while no other material cost more than $4.00.
The shingles and the bricks cost $4.00 each, more than the $3.90 spent on nails.
Thoreau spent only $0.01 on chalk, the least he spent on any material.

items.explanation: To show that boards cost the most, the boards must be compared with every other material. The boards cost $8.03½, and the next highest costs in the table are $4.00, so this choice supports the claim.

rationales.A: These figures are accurate, but comparing the boards with the total does not show that they cost more than each other material.
rationales.C: This compares other materials with one another and says nothing about the boards.
rationales.D: Identifying the least expensive material does not show which one was most expensive.

passage.intro: The following text is from Henry David Thoreau's 1854 book Walden. Thoreau built the house himself near Walden Pond in Massachusetts.
passage.text: I have thus a tight shingled and plastered house, ten feet wide by fifteen long, and eight-feet posts, with a garret and a closet, a large window on each side, two trap doors, one door at the end, and a brick fireplace opposite.

table.title: Darwin's estimates of earth brought to the surface by worms
columns: Dry earth per acre in one year (tons)
rows: Old terrace at Leith Hill Place

data.label: Charles Darwin, The Formation of Vegetable Mould, through the Action of Worms (1881)

items.context: The table shows estimates Darwin made at four sites by weighing the castings (soil that worms bring to the surface) collected over a period of time.
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Darwin's claim?

choices.text: At two of the three sites in England, the estimate is more than 10 tons of earth per acre in a year.
At every site in the table, the estimate is more than 10 tons of earth per acre in a year.
At the site near Nice, in France, the estimate is more than 14 tons of earth per acre in a year.
The old terrace at Leith Hill Place has the smallest estimate of the four sites in the table.

items.explanation: Darwin claims that in “many parts of England” more than ten tons of earth pass through worms on each acre every year. Two of the three English sites, at 18.12 and 16.1 tons, are above ten tons, which supports a claim about many parts, though not all, of England.

rationales.B: This is inaccurate, because the terrace at Leith Hill Place is estimated at only 7.56 tons.
rationales.C: This is accurate, but Nice is in France, and Darwin's claim concerns England.
rationales.D: This is accurate, but a site below ten tons does not support a claim that many places exceed ten tons.

passage.intro: The following text is from Charles Darwin's 1881 book The Formation of Vegetable Mould, through the Action of Worms.
passage.text: In many parts of England a weight of more than ten tons (10,516 kilogrammes) of dry earth annually passes through their bodies and is brought to the surface on each acre of land; so that the whole superficial bed of vegetable mould passes through their bodies in the course of every few years.

source.author: Charles Darwin
source.title: The Formation of Vegetable Mould, through the Action of Worms

table.title: Thoreau's bean field accounts for one season
rows: Horse cultivator and boy three hours
Horse and cart to get crop
Nine bushels and twelve quarts of beans sold

items.context: Thoreau recorded his costs, which he called outgoes, and his income. A student claims that the field earned a profit mainly because of the beans Thoreau sold.
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the student's claim?

choices.text: His total income of $23.44 was greater than his total outgoes of $14.72½.
Plowing, harrowing, and furrowing cost $7.50, more than any other outgo.
The beans he sold brought in $16.94, by itself more than his total outgoes of $14.72½.
He earned $2.50 from large potatoes and $2.25 from small potatoes.

items.explanation: If the bean sales alone, $16.94, exceeded all the outgoes, $14.72½, then the beans by themselves were enough to make the field profitable. That supports the claim that the profit came mainly from beans.

rationales.A: This shows that the field made a profit, but not that the beans were the main reason.
rationales.B: This identifies the largest cost, which says nothing about where the profit came from.
rationales.D: This describes income from potatoes, which does not show that beans produced the profit.

passage.intro: The following text is from Henry David Thoreau's 1854 book Walden. Thoreau farmed a field near his cabin for one season.
passage.text:
I harvested twelve bushels of beans.

But to be more particular, for it is complained that Mr. Coleman has reported chiefly the expensive experiments of gentlemen farmers, my outgoes were . . .

items.originalText: The naturalist Gilbert White recorded the rain that fell each year in the village of Selborne, England. His records show how widely rainfall there could vary from one year to the next: the wettest of these years brought nearly twice as much rain as the driest year.

figure.title: Rainfall at Selborne, England, 1780–1786
figure.note: Data: Gilbert White, The Natural History and Antiquities of Selborne (1789). Each year ran from January 1 to January 1.

items.blank: the wettest of these years brought nearly twice as much rain as the driest year
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.text: rainfall rose steadily every year from 1780 to 1786
the wettest of these years brought nearly twice as much rain as the driest year
the rainfall in 1783 was nearly the same as the rainfall in 1784
no year in these records brought less than 30 inches of rain

items.explanation: The statement is about how widely rainfall varied. The wettest year, 1782, had 50.26 inches, and the driest, 1780, had 27.32 inches, so the wettest year brought nearly twice as much rain.

rationales.A: Rainfall fell from 1782 to 1783 and again from 1784 to 1785, so it did not rise every year.
rationales.C: This is accurate, but two nearly equal years show how little rainfall changed, not how widely it varied.
rationales.D: This is inaccurate, because 1780 brought only 27.32 inches.

items.originalText: Charles Darwin weighed the castings, small piles of soil that earthworms leave at the mouths of their burrows. A colleague, Dr. King, collected castings for him in two very different places: near Nice, in France, and in the Nilgiri Mountains of southern India. A student claims that King's castings from the Nilgiri Mountains were more than twice as heavy, on average, as his castings from near Nice.

table.title: Weight of dried castings from single burrows
rows: 1 large casting from a level field

data.label: Charles Darwin, The Formation of Vegetable Mould, through the Action of Worms (1881)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the student's claim?

choices.text: The castings from Lower Bengal averaged 1.24 ounces, less than the castings from near Nice.
The Nilgiri castings averaged 3.15 ounces, the greatest average weight of any place in the table.
The castings from near Nice averaged 1.37 ounces, more than the 1.22-ounce casting from Down.
The Nilgiri castings averaged 3.15 ounces, more than twice the 1.37-ounce average from near Nice.

items.explanation: The claim compares King's two sites. Since 2 × 1.37 = 2.74, and 3.15 is greater than 2.74, the Nilgiri average is more than twice the Nice average.

rationales.A: This is accurate, but Lower Bengal is not one of the two sites the claim compares.
rationales.B: This is accurate, but being the greatest does not show that the Nilgiri castings were more than twice as heavy as those from Nice.
rationales.C: This compares Nice with Down, England, which is not part of the claim.

items.blank: only served to inspire me with a desire and determination to learn
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: led me to give up any hope of learning to read on my own
convinced me that reading would bring me no good, but much harm
persuaded my mistress to secretly begin teaching me once more
only served to inspire me with a desire and determination to learn

items.explanation: Douglass sets up a pattern of opposites: what his enslaver dreaded, he desired; what was evil to the enslaver was good to him. The enslaver's argument against reading should therefore have the opposite effect and strengthen Douglass's wish to learn.

rationales.A: This breaks the pattern of opposites, since the enslaver's warning would then have worked as intended.
rationales.B: This repeats the enslaver's view as if Douglass accepted it, contradicting the reversal the text builds.
rationales.C: The text describes only Douglass's own response, and nothing suggests his mistress changed her mind.

passage.intro: The following text is from Frederick Douglass's 1845 autobiography Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave. Douglass has just overheard his enslaver warn that teaching him to read would make him impossible to control.
passage.text: The very decided manner with which he spoke, and strove to impress his wife with the evil consequences of giving me instruction, served to convince me that he was deeply sensible of the truths he was uttering. . . . What he most dreaded, that I most desired. What he most loved, that I most hated. That which to him was a great evil, to be carefully shunned, was to me a great good, to be diligently sought; and the argument which he so warmly urged, against my learning to read, only served to inspire me with a desire and determination to learn.

source.author: Frederick Douglass
source.title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave

items.blank: for I had to finish whatever I began
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: because my mother allowed me only simple shapes
for I had to finish whatever I began
since complex patterns used too few beads
because simple designs were what my playmates wanted

items.explanation: The narrator says long designs used up “many a sunny hour” and calls the lesson “self-inflicted punishment.” The punishment makes sense only if she had to complete every design she started.

rationales.A: The text says her mother required original designs, so it does not suggest a rule against complex ones.
rationales.C: Nothing in the text connects the number of beads to the narrator's choice of patterns.
rationales.D: The text never mentions what her playmates wanted, so this does not explain the narrator's punishment.

passage.intro: The following text is from Zitkala-Ša's 1921 book American Indian Stories. She recalls learning beadwork from her mother as a child.
passage.text: It took many trials before I learned how to knot my sinew thread on the point of my finger, as I saw her do. Then the next difficulty was in keeping my thread stiffly twisted, so that I could easily string my beads upon it. My mother required of me original designs for my lessons in beading. At first I frequently ensnared many a sunny hour into working a long design. Soon I learned from self-inflicted punishment to refrain from drawing complex patterns, for I had to finish whatever I began.

items.blank: proof of the high development of Some Where Else
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: proof of the high development of Some Where Else
a threat that had to be driven away at once
a natural event that needed no further explanation
a sign that the ancient records of other peoples were false

items.explanation: The people had already inferred that advanced civilizations existed elsewhere. A flying machine from outside would therefore confirm that inference, which also explains why they prepared to receive the visitors.

rationales.B: The text says they prepared to receive the visitors “cautiously and eagerly,” not to drive them away.
rationales.C: A people “keen on inference and deduction” would draw a conclusion from the biplane rather than dismiss it.
rationales.D: Their records already told them of other peoples, so an aircraft from elsewhere would support those records.

passage.intro: The following text is from Charlotte Perkins Gilman's 1915 novel Herland. The narrator describes the people of a country that had long been cut off from the rest of the world.
passage.text:
[They] had inferred (marvelously keen on inference and deduction their minds were!) the existence and development of civilization in other places, much as we infer it on other planets.

When our biplane came whirring over their heads in that first scouting flight of ours, they had instantly accepted it as proof of the high development of Some Where Else, and had prepared to receive us as cautiously and eagerly as we might prepare to welcome visitors who came “by meteor” from Mars.

items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: more than 4,500,000 years
about 4,566 years
less than 4,500,000 years
about 748 years

items.explanation: If the land is lowered 1 foot every 4,566 years and its average height is 748 feet, wearing it all away takes about 748 × 4,566, or roughly 3.4 million years. That is less than 4,500,000 years.

rationales.A: This uses the right figure but the wrong direction, since about 3.4 million years is less than 4.5 million.
rationales.B: This is the time needed to lower the land by only 1 foot, not by its full height.
rationales.D: This is the land's average height in feet, not a length of time.

passage.intro: The following text is from Charles Darwin's 1881 book The Formation of Vegetable Mould, through the Action of Worms. Darwin uses a river to show how quickly running water can wear land away.
passage.text: For the sake of those who have never attended to this subject, a single instance may be here given, namely, that of the Mississippi, which is chosen because the amount of sediment brought down by this great river has been investigated with especial care by order of the United States Government. The result is, as Mr. Croll shows, that the mean level of its enormous area of drainage must be lowered 1/4566 of a foot annually, or 1 foot in 4566 years. Consequently, taking the best estimate of the mean height of the North American continent, viz. 748 feet, and looking to the future, the whole of the great Mississippi basin will be washed away, and “brought down to the sea-level in less than 4,500,000 years, if no elevation of the land takes place.”

source.author: Charles Darwin
source.title: The Formation of Vegetable Mould, through the Action of Worms

items.blank: he was glad each time when he was not selected
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: he barked at each stranger until he was chosen
he was glad each time when he was not selected
he hoped that the next stranger would take him
he tried to show the strangers how strong he was

items.explanation: The dogs taken away never came back, and Buck feared the future. A dog in that position would be relieved, not eager, each time he was passed over.

rationales.A: Buck fears where the dogs go, so he would not try to get himself chosen.
rationales.C: Hoping to be taken conflicts with the “fear of the future” the text says was strong upon him.
rationales.D: Showing off his strength would make him more likely to be chosen, which a fearful Buck would avoid.

passage.intro: The following text is from Jack London's 1903 novel The Call of the Wild. Buck, a dog, has been taken from his home and sold to a man in a red sweater.
passage.text: Now and again men came, strangers, who talked excitedly, wheedlingly, and in all kinds of fashions to the man in the red sweater. And at such times that money passed between them the strangers took one or more of the dogs away with them. Buck wondered where they went, for they never came back; but the fear of the future was strong upon him, and he was glad each time when he was not selected.

items.blank: like some folks that had it hard in their youth
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: like some folks that never left their own dooryards
like a garden that was tended every single day
like some folks that had it hard in their youth
like the weeds that crowd out every other plant

items.explanation: Mrs. Todd says the tansy grew better for being trampled. The comparison should describe something that grows stronger because of early hardship, and the rest of the sentence describes people “bound to make the most of themselves.”

rationales.A: Staying at home is not a hardship that makes someone stronger, so it does not match being “scuffed down.”
rationales.B: Daily care is the opposite of being trampled all spring, so the comparison would not fit.
rationales.D: Weeds that crowd out other plants do not match the rest of the sentence, which describes people making the most of themselves.

passage.intro: The following text is from Sarah Orne Jewett's 1896 novel The Country of the Pointed Firs. Mrs. Todd gathers herbs, such as tansy, to make medicines.
passage.text: One day she appeared at the schoolhouse itself, partly out of amused curiosity about my industries; but she explained that there was no tansy in the neighborhood with such snap to it as some that grew about the schoolhouse lot. Being scuffed down all the spring made it grow so much the better, like some folks that had it hard in their youth, and were bound to make the most of themselves before they died.

source.author: Sarah Orne Jewett
source.title: The Country of the Pointed Firs

items.blank: I hoped Mr. Bixby would change the subject
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: I resolved to write each point's name in my notebook
I hoped Mr. Bixby would change the subject
I began to admire the beauty of each one
I realized that every point was worth remembering

items.explanation: Twain could not see “the bearing” of the information, did not think it mattered to him, and found the points dull and alike. A bored learner who sees no use in the lesson would hope the teacher would talk about something else.

rationales.A: Taking careful notes would show he valued the information, but he says it was of no interest to him.
rationales.C: He calls the points “monotonously unpicturesque,” so he did not find them beautiful.
rationales.D: At this point he cannot see why the points matter, so he has not yet realized their value.

passage.intro: The following text is from Mark Twain's 1883 memoir Life on the Mississippi. As a young man, Twain is learning from Mr. Bixby how to pilot a steamboat.
passage.text: Now and then Mr. Bixby called my attention to certain things. Said he, 'This is Six-Mile Point.' I assented. It was pleasant enough information, but I could not see the bearing of it. I was not conscious that it was a matter of any interest to me. Another time he said, 'This is Nine-Mile Point.' Later he said, 'This is Twelve-Mile Point.' They were all about level with the water's edge; they all looked about alike to me; they were monotonously unpicturesque. I hoped Mr. Bixby would change the subject.

items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “pronounced” most nearly mean?

choices.text: spoken aloud
officially declared
clearly noticeable
carefully planned

items.explanation: The narrator says the pattern is dull enough to confuse the eye yet “pronounced enough to constantly irritate.” Something that keeps irritating the eye must stand out, so “pronounced” means clearly noticeable.

rationales.A: “Pronounced” can describe a spoken word, but a wallpaper pattern is seen, not spoken.
rationales.B: Nothing in the text involves an official announcement about the pattern.
rationales.D: The narrator says the curves “commit suicide” and end in “contradictions,” so the pattern does not seem carefully planned.

passage.intro: The following text is from Charlotte Perkins Gilman's 1892 short story “The Yellow Wallpaper.” The narrator describes the pattern of the wallpaper in her room.
passage.text: It is dull enough to confuse the eye in following, pronounced enough to constantly irritate and provoke study, and when you follow the lame uncertain curves for a little distance they suddenly commit suicide—plunge off at outrageous angles, destroy themselves in unheard of contradictions.

items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.text: faint hope
false hope
high hope
borrowed hope

items.explanation: “Though conscious of the difficulty” sets up a contrast: despite knowing how hard it would be, Douglass set out with strong hope and a “fixed purpose.” “High hope” fits that contrast.

rationales.A: Faint hope would match the difficulty instead of contrasting with it, and it clashes with his “fixed purpose.”
rationales.B: False hope would mean he expected to fail, which conflicts with his firm resolve to learn.
rationales.D: Hope cannot sensibly be borrowed here, and nothing suggests his hope came from someone else.

passage.intro: The following text is from Frederick Douglass's 1845 autobiography. His enslaver has just forbidden anyone to teach him to read.
passage.text: Whilst I was saddened by the thought of losing the aid of my kind mistress, I was gladdened by the invaluable instruction which, by the merest accident, I had gained from my master. Though conscious of the difficulty of learning without a teacher, I set out with high hope, and a fixed purpose, at whatever cost of trouble, to learn how to read.

source.author: Frederick Douglass
source.title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave

items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “deliberately” most nearly mean?

choices.text: at a slow and careful pace
with conscious purpose
without telling anyone
in order to make money

items.explanation: Thoreau wants to “front only the essential facts of life” and not discover at death “that I had not lived.” To live deliberately is to live with careful attention and intention.

rationales.A: “Deliberately” can describe an unhurried pace, but Thoreau's concern is living with intention, not living at a slow speed.
rationales.C: Nothing in the text suggests Thoreau is hiding his purpose from anyone.
rationales.D: Nothing in the text concerns earning money; his aim is to learn what life has to teach.

passage.intro: The following text is from Henry David Thoreau's 1854 book Walden, in which he describes two years he spent living in a small cabin near Walden Pond in Massachusetts.
passage.text: I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived. I did not wish to live what was not life, living is so dear; nor did I wish to practise resignation, unless it was quite necessary.

items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “rigorously” most nearly mean?

choices.text: harshly
quickly
secretly
strictly

items.explanation: The cats were produced by “prolonged and careful selection and exclusion,” and they were bred to hunt pests but leave birds alone. “Rigorously” here means strictly and exactly controlled.

rationales.A: “Rigorous” can suggest severity, but the text stresses careful, exact control rather than harsh treatment of the cats.
rationales.B: The breeding is described as “prolonged,” the opposite of quick.
rationales.C: The narrator calls the result “a fact” and describes it openly; nothing about the breeding was hidden.

passage.intro: The following text is from Charlotte Perkins Gilman's 1915 novel Herland. The narrator describes the cats raised by the women of an isolated country.
passage.text:
What do you suppose these Lady Burbanks had done with their cats? By the most prolonged and careful selection and exclusion they had developed a race of cats that did not sing! That's a fact. The most those poor dumb brutes could do was to make a kind of squeak when they were hungry or wanted the door open, and, of course, to purr, and make the various mother-noises to their kittens.

Moreover, they had ceased to kill birds. They were rigorously bred to destroy mice and moles and all such enemies of the food supply; but the birds were numerous and safe.

items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “unwonted” most nearly mean?

choices.text: unwanted
unusual
unpaid
unfair

items.explanation: The price of dogs had been “boomed skyward” by the demand, so the demand must have been far beyond what was normal. “Unwonted” means unusual or not customary.

rationales.A: The word looks like “unwanted,” but the dogs were very much wanted; that is why prices rose.
rationales.C: The demand drove prices up, so it had nothing to do with going unpaid.
rationales.D: The text says the price was “not an unfair sum,” so fairness is not what “unwonted” describes.

passage.intro: The following text is from Jack London's 1903 novel The Call of the Wild. Perrault, a courier for the Canadian government, has just bought Buck, a dog, during the Klondike gold rush.
passage.text: Perrault grinned. Considering that the price of dogs had been boomed skyward by the unwonted demand, it was not an unfair sum for so fine an animal. The Canadian Government would be no loser, nor would its despatches travel the slower. Perrault knew dogs, and when he looked at Buck he knew that he was one in a thousand—"One in ten t'ousand," he commented mentally.

items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.text: unite
refuse
conceal
outgrow

items.explanation: Emma is handsome, clever, rich, well housed, and cheerful, so she seems to bring together, or unite, many of life's best blessings.

rationales.B: Emma has all these advantages, so she has not refused them.
rationales.C: Nothing suggests Emma hides her advantages; the text lists them openly.
rationales.D: The text says she has lived nearly twenty-one years with little to distress her, so she has not outgrown her blessings.

passage.intro: The following text is from Jane Austen's 1815 novel Emma.
passage.text: Emma Woodhouse, handsome, clever, and rich, with a comfortable home and happy disposition, seemed to unite some of the best blessings of existence; and had lived nearly twenty-one years in the world with very little to distress or vex her.

items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.text: celebrate
describe
conceal
train

items.explanation: The sentence pairs two actions as art's aim: to reveal art and to do the opposite to the artist. The opposite of revealing is concealing.

rationales.A: Celebrating the artist would put the artist forward, which works against the contrast with “reveal art.”
rationales.B: Describing the artist would also reveal the artist, so it does not form the contrast the sentence sets up.
rationales.D: Training the artist has nothing to do with what a work of art shows or hides.

passage.intro: The following text is from the preface to Oscar Wilde's 1891 novel The Picture of Dorian Gray.
passage.text: The artist is the creator of beautiful things. To reveal art and conceal the artist is art's aim. The critic is he who can translate into another manner or a new material his impression of beautiful things.

items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “concerns” most nearly mean?

choices.text: worries
matters to
belongs to
describes

items.explanation: Faraday is explaining what his audience needs to understand next: “It concerns us much to know” means it matters a great deal to us to know.

rationales.A: “Concerns” can mean worries, but Faraday is not anxious; he is pointing out what is important to learn.
rationales.C: The flame's shape does not belong to the audience; the point is that knowing it is important.
rationales.D: The sentence is about why knowing the flame's shape is important, not about a description.

passage.intro: The following text is from Michael Faraday's 1861 book The Chemical History of a Candle, based on lectures he gave to young people.
passage.text: Now, as to the shape or form of the flame. It concerns us much to know about the condition which the matter of the candle finally assumes at the top of the wick—where you have such beauty and brightness as nothing but combustion or flame can produce.

source.author: Michael Faraday
source.title: The Chemical History of a Candle

items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.text: criticized
tolerated
abandoned
cherished

items.explanation: Conservatives valued the small, inconvenient Academy because it kept out the “new people” they dreaded, and the sentence goes on to say others “clung to it.” “Cherished” fits this fond attachment.

rationales.A: The conservatives liked what the Academy's smallness did for them, so they would not criticize it for that.
rationales.B: Tolerating suggests putting up with something disliked, but the text gives a reason they actively valued the Academy.
rationales.C: The world of fashion still gathered there every winter, so it had not been abandoned.

passage.intro: The following text is from Edith Wharton's 1920 novel The Age of Innocence, set in New York City in the 1870s. The Academy was the city's opera house.
passage.text: Though there was already talk of the erection, in remote metropolitan distances "above the Forties," of a new Opera House which should compete in costliness and splendour with those of the great European capitals, the world of fashion was still content to reassemble every winter in the shabby red and gold boxes of the sociable old Academy. Conservatives cherished it for being small and inconvenient, and thus keeping out the "new people" whom New York was beginning to dread and yet be drawn to; and the sentimental clung to it for its historic associations, and the musical for its excellent acoustics, always so problematic a quality in halls built for the hearing of music.

items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.text: dangerous
harmless
hungry
gigantic

items.explanation: Mary is not frightened because the snake “would not hurt her.” The word must describe a creature that poses no danger: harmless.

rationales.A: A dangerous snake would give Mary a reason to be frightened, not a reason to stay calm.
rationales.C: A hungry snake does not explain why Mary is unafraid, and the snake seems only in a hurry to leave.
rationales.D: The text calls it a “little” snake, so it cannot be gigantic.

passage.intro: The following text is from Frances Hodgson Burnett's 1911 novel The Secret Garden. Mary, a young girl, has been left alone in her family's house in India.
passage.text: But no one came, and as she lay waiting the house seemed to grow more and more silent. She heard something rustling on the matting and when she looked down she saw a little snake gliding along and watching her with eyes like jewels. She was not frightened, because he was a harmless little thing who would not hurt her and he seemed in a hurry to get out of the room. He slipped under the door as she watched him.

items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “altered” most nearly mean?

choices.text: repaired
angry
changed
loud

items.explanation: After a minute of silence, Meg speaks seriously about the family's sacrifices. Her tone has shifted from the earlier conversation: “altered” means changed.

rationales.A: “Altered” can describe clothing that has been fixed, but a tone of voice is not repaired.
rationales.B: Meg speaks about sacrifice and admits her own regret, which is serious and sad rather than angry.
rationales.D: Nothing suggests Meg raises her voice; she speaks after a quiet moment.

passage.intro: The following text is from Louisa May Alcott's 1868 novel Little Women. The four March sisters are talking about Christmas while their father is away serving in the Civil War.
passage.text: Nobody spoke for a minute; then Meg said in an altered tone, "You know the reason Mother proposed not having any presents this Christmas was because it is going to be a hard winter for everyone; and she thinks we ought not to spend money for pleasure, when our men are suffering so in the army. We can't do much, but we can make our little sacrifices, and ought to do it gladly. But I am afraid I don't," and Meg shook her head, as she thought regretfully of all the pretty things she wanted.

items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It describes a set of labels used in a shipyard and then explains why carpenters needed each one.
It describes a problem the narrator faced and then explains why he decided not to pursue it.
It explains where the narrator found a way to learn, gives examples of it, and then tells how he used it.
It compares the narrator's early attempts at writing with the carpenters' finished work on the ships.

items.explanation: Douglass first says the idea for learning to write came from watching shipyard carpenters, then gives examples of their letter labels, and finally tells how he learned and copied those letters.

rationales.A: The labels are described, but the text's point is how they taught Douglass to write, not why carpenters needed them.
rationales.B: Douglass does not give up; the text ends with him able to make the four letters.
rationales.D: The text never compares his writing with the carpenters' work.

passage.intro: The following text is from Frederick Douglass's 1845 autobiography. As a boy, Douglass lived near a shipyard in Baltimore.
passage.text: The idea as to how I might learn to write was suggested to me by being in Durgin and Bailey's ship-yard, and frequently seeing the ship carpenters, after hewing, and getting a piece of timber ready for use, write on the timber the name of that part of the ship for which it was intended. When a piece of timber was intended for the larboard side, it would be marked thus—“L.” When a piece was for the starboard side, it would be marked thus—“S.” . . . I soon learned the names of these letters, and for what they were intended when placed upon a piece of timber in the ship-yard. I immediately commenced copying them, and in a short time was able to make the four letters named.

source.author: Frederick Douglass
source.title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave

items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.text: To explain why operas were translated into Italian for audiences in New York
To show, with gentle irony, how readily Newland Archer accepts the customs of his social world
To argue that the customs of New York society made little sense to anyone who lived there
To describe the clothing and grooming habits that were fashionable among young men in New York

items.explanation: The text calls an absurd translation rule “unalterable and unquestioned,” then says it seemed as natural to Archer as his monogrammed brushes and buttonhole flower. The point is Archer's easy acceptance of his world's conventions.

rationales.A: The translation rule is presented as an absurd example of a convention, not explained as a practice.
rationales.C: The text says these customs seemed natural to Archer, so it does not claim they made no sense to the people who lived there.
rationales.D: The brushes and flower are examples of conventions Archer accepts, not the subject of the text.

passage.intro: The following text is from Edith Wharton's 1920 novel The Age of Innocence. Newland Archer is attending an opera in New York City.
passage.text: She sang, of course, "M'ama!" and not "he loves me," since an unalterable and unquestioned law of the musical world required that the German text of French operas sung by Swedish artists should be translated into Italian for the clearer understanding of English-speaking audiences. This seemed as natural to Newland Archer as all the other conventions on which his life was moulded: such as the duty of using two silver-backed brushes with his monogram in blue enamel to part his hair, and of never appearing in society without a flower (preferably a gardenia) in his buttonhole.

items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It describes the lake's shore and then explains why the lake was given the Indian name that it has.
It explains how glaciers form and then traces the history of a single glacier.
It compares two mountain lakes and then concludes which of them is older.
It describes the bare rock around a lake and then suggests how the lake's basin was formed.

items.explanation: Muir first describes the shore of bare, shining granite and then offers an explanation for the basin: it “seems to have been slowly excavated by the ancient glaciers.”

rationales.A: The name is mentioned as it relates to the shining rock, but the text ends by explaining how the basin formed, not by explaining the name.
rationales.B: Muir does not explain how glaciers form or follow one glacier's history.
rationales.C: Only one lake is described.

passage.intro: The following text is from John Muir's 1911 book My First Summer in the Sierra. Muir describes a lake in the Sierra Nevada mountains.
passage.text: Scarce a handful of loose soil is to be seen on the north shore. All is bare, shining granite, suggesting the Indian name of the lake, Pywiack, meaning shining rock. The basin seems to have been slowly excavated by the ancient glaciers, a marvelous work requiring countless thousands of years.

source.author: John Muir
source.title: My First Summer in the Sierra

items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.text: To describe the private feelings of a wealthy man as he settles into a new neighbourhood
To present a widely held belief and show how it shapes a community's view of a newcomer
To argue that wealthy men should marry soon after moving to a new place
To explain why the families in a neighbourhood tend to avoid newcomers until they know them

items.explanation: The text states a “truth universally acknowledged” and then shows its effect: whatever the man himself feels, local families already treat him as the “rightful property” of one of their daughters.

rationales.A: The text says the man's feelings may be “little known,” so it does not describe them.
rationales.C: The text reports what people believe; it does not argue for what wealthy men should do.
rationales.D: The families are eager to claim the newcomer, not to avoid him.

passage.intro: The following text is from the opening of Jane Austen's 1813 novel Pride and Prejudice.
passage.text:
It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.

However little known the feelings or views of such a man may be on his first entering a neighbourhood, this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families, that he is considered the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters.

items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.text: It names the event that causes the sorrow described in the first sentence.
It introduces a new character whose arrival changes Emma's household.
It shows that Emma had expected the wedding for a long time.
It explains why Emma's father falls asleep after dinner.

items.explanation: The first sentence says that sorrow came, and the underlined sentence names its cause: Miss Taylor's marriage. The rest of the text describes Emma's loss on the wedding day.

rationales.B: Miss Taylor is not new; the text describes her as Emma's “beloved friend” of long standing.
rationales.C: The text says this was the first time Emma thought about what would continue, so it does not suggest long expectation.
rationales.D: Her father falls asleep “as usual,” which the marriage does not cause.

passage.intro: The following text is from Jane Austen's 1815 novel Emma. Miss Taylor had lived with Emma's family for sixteen years as Emma's governess and friend.
passage.text: Sorrow came—a gentle sorrow—but not at all in the shape of any disagreeable consciousness.—Miss Taylor married. It was Miss Taylor's loss which first brought grief. It was on the wedding-day of this beloved friend that Emma first sat in mournful thought of any continuance. The wedding over, and the bride-people gone, her father and herself were left to dine together, with no prospect of a third to cheer a long evening. Her father composed himself to sleep after dinner, as usual, and she had then only to sit and think of what she had lost.

items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It lists the skills the narrator gained and then shows the overconfidence those skills produced.
It describes the narrator's mistakes as a pilot and then explains how he corrected them.
It compares the narrator's training with that of other pilots on the river.
It traces the route of the river from St. Louis to New Orleans, landmark by landmark.

items.explanation: A long series of “when I had” clauses lists what the narrator learned. Then he judges his education complete and starts wearing his cap tilted and a toothpick in his mouth, and Mr. Bixby notices “these airs.”

rationales.B: The text lists what he mastered, not mistakes he made and corrected.
rationales.C: No other pilots are mentioned.
rationales.D: The two cities are named only to show how well he knew the river, not to trace the route.

passage.intro: The following text is from Mark Twain's 1883 memoir Life on the Mississippi. Twain is training to pilot steamboats under Mr. Bixby.
passage.text: When I had learned the name and position of every visible feature of the river; when I had so mastered its shape that I could shut my eyes and trace it from St. Louis to New Orleans; when I had learned to read the face of the water as one would cull the news from the morning paper; and finally, when I had trained my dull memory to treasure up an endless array of soundings and crossing-marks, and keep fast hold of them, I judged that my education was complete: so I got to tilting my cap to the side of my head, and wearing a tooth-pick in my mouth at the wheel. Mr. Bixby had his eye on these airs.

items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.text: To describe the people who walked in the funeral procession
To explain why the funeral was held on the edge of the shore
To criticize the villagers for holding a funeral on such a beautiful day
To contrast a small human event with the vast and lively natural world around it

items.explanation: The procession looks “futile and helpless” against the islands, the sea, and the clear sky, and the sparrows sing as if in “contempt” for concern with death. The text sets the small human scene against the vast landscape.

rationales.A: The text calls the procession small and helpless but does not describe the individual people in it.
rationales.B: The text does not explain where or why the funeral was held.
rationales.C: The contempt belongs to the singing sparrows; the narrator does not criticize the villagers.

passage.intro: The following text is from Sarah Orne Jewett's 1896 novel The Country of the Pointed Firs. The narrator is watching a funeral procession walk along the coast.
passage.text: The bay-sheltered islands and the great sea beyond stretched away to the far horizon southward and eastward; the little procession in the foreground looked futile and helpless on the edge of the rocky shore. It was a glorious day early in July, with a clear, high sky; there were no clouds, there was no noise of the sea. The song sparrows sang and sang, as if with joyous knowledge of immortality, and contempt for those who could so pettily concern themselves with death. I stood watching until the funeral procession had crept round a shoulder of the slope below and disappeared from the great landscape as if it had gone into a cave.

source.author: Sarah Orne Jewett
source.title: The Country of the Pointed Firs

items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It explains how the man came to be in the churchyard and why he needs help.
It builds a description of a man through a series of details and ends with his seizing the narrator.
It describes the churchyard in detail and then introduces the man who appears in it.
It compares the man's appearance with the narrator's own appearance.

items.explanation: The text piles up details about the man's appearance and what he has suffered, then ends with an action: his teeth chatter “as he seized me by the chin.”

rationales.A: The text describes the man but never explains how he got there or what he wants.
rationales.C: The churchyard itself is not described; every detail is about the man.
rationales.D: The narrator does not describe his own appearance.

passage.intro: The following text is from Charles Dickens's 1861 novel Great Expectations. Pip, a young boy, is alone in a churchyard when a stranger appears.
passage.text: A fearful man, all in coarse gray, with a great iron on his leg. A man with no hat, and with broken shoes, and with an old rag tied round his head. A man who had been soaked in water, and smothered in mud, and lamed by stones, and cut by flints, and stung by nettles, and torn by briars; who limped, and shivered, and glared, and growled; and whose teeth chattered in his head as he seized me by the chin.

items.stem: Based on the texts, how would Darwin (Text 2) most likely respond to White's claim (Text 1) that earthworms, despite their appearance, are important?

choices.text: He would say White exaggerates, since worms affect only soil and not the history of the land.
He would agree and go further, suggesting that worms have worked the land since before humans existed.
He would disagree, arguing that ploughing by people has done more to improve the soil than worms have.
He would agree only about the birds and other animals that White says depend on worms for food.

items.explanation: White says worms are a “despicable” link in nature only in appearance. Darwin agrees and goes further: worms ploughed the land “long before” humans existed and have played a very important part “in the history of the world.”

rationales.A: Darwin says worms have played an important part in the history of the world, so he would not call White's claim exaggerated.
rationales.C: Darwin mentions the plough only to say that worms were ploughing the land long before people were.
rationales.D: Darwin's text does not discuss birds and other animals, and his agreement with White is much broader than that.

passages.intro: Text 1 is from a 1777 letter by the English naturalist Gilbert White, published in his 1789 book The Natural History and Antiquities of Selborne.
passages.text: Earth-worms, though in appearance a small and despicable link in the chain of nature, yet, if lost, would make a lamentable chasm. For, to say nothing of half the birds, and some quadrupeds, which are almost entirely supported by them, worms seem to be the great promoters of vegetation, which would proceed but lamely without them, by boring, perforating, and loosening the soil, and rendering it pervious to rains and the fibres of plants . . .

source.author: Gilbert White
source.title: The Natural History and Antiquities of Selborne

passages.intro: Text 2 is from Charles Darwin's 1881 book The Formation of Vegetable Mould, through the Action of Worms.
passages.text: The plough is one of the most ancient and most valuable of man’s inventions; but long before he existed the land was in fact regularly ploughed, and still continues to be thus ploughed by earth-worms. It may be doubted whether there are many other animals which have played so important a part in the history of the world, as have these lowly organized creatures.

items.stem: Based on the texts, how would Faraday (Text 2) most likely respond to Twain's view (Text 1) that learning how something works can take away its beauty?

choices.text: He would agree, since he says a flame's light depends on dirty solid particles such as charcoal.
He would agree that doctors stop seeing beauty but argue that scientists never do.
He would disagree, arguing that beauty is something only trained experts can truly see.
He would disagree, since he finds the very process that makes a flame bright beautiful to think about.

items.explanation: Twain says the river's beauty vanished once he learned to read it for piloting. Faraday asks, “Is it not beautiful to think that such a process is going on,” finding beauty in the very workings he explains.

rationales.A: Faraday does call charcoal dirty, but he says it becomes part of a “glorious and beautiful light,” which is the opposite of Twain's view.
rationales.B: Faraday says nothing about doctors, and Text 2 makes no claim about what all scientists see.
rationales.C: Faraday finds understanding beautiful, but he never says that only experts can see beauty.

passages.intro: Text 1 is from Mark Twain's 1883 memoir Life on the Mississippi, which describes his years learning to pilot steamboats.
passages.text: No, the romance and the beauty were all gone from the river. All the value any feature of it had for me now was the amount of usefulness it could furnish toward compassing the safe piloting of a steamboat. Since those days, I have pitied doctors from my heart. What does the lovely flush in a beauty's cheek mean to a doctor but a 'break' that ripples above some deadly disease. Are not all her visible charms sown thick with what are to him the signs and symbols of hidden decay? Does he ever see her beauty at all, or doesn't he simply view her professionally, and comment upon her unwholesome condition all to himself? And doesn't he sometimes wonder whether he has gained most or lost most by learning his trade?

passages.intro: Text 2 is from Michael Faraday's 1861 book The Chemical History of a Candle, based on lectures that explained the chemistry of a burning candle.
passages.text: Is it not beautiful to think that such a process is going on, and that such a dirty thing as charcoal can become so incandescent? You see it comes to this—that all bright flames contain these solid particles; all things that burn and produce solid particles, either during the time they are burning, as in the candle, or immediately after being burnt, as in the case of the gunpowder and iron-filings,—all these things give us this glorious and beautiful light.

source.author: Michael Faraday
source.title: The Chemical History of a Candle

items.stem: Based on the texts, how would Du Bois (Text 2) most likely respond to Washington's statement (Text 1) that “there is as much dignity in tilling a field as in writing a poem”?

choices.text: He would agree and add that writing poetry distracts people from making economic progress.
He would argue that farming deserves less respect than other kinds of work.
He would argue that Washington's focus on labor and money crowds out the higher aims of life.
He would agree but argue that Washington underestimates how quickly the South's economy is growing.

items.explanation: Du Bois says Washington's program becomes “a gospel of Work and Money” that nearly overshadows “the higher aims of life.” He would see Washington's praise of field work as part of that narrow focus.

rationales.A: Du Bois worries that higher aims are being overshadowed, so he would not dismiss pursuits such as poetry.
rationales.B: Du Bois criticizes the emphasis of Washington's program, not the dignity of farming itself.
rationales.D: Du Bois calls the period one of “unusual economic development,” but he does not say Washington misjudges its pace.

passages.intro: Text 1 is from a speech Booker T. Washington gave in Atlanta in 1895, printed in his 1901 autobiography Up from Slavery.
passages.text: Our greatest danger is that in the great leap from slavery to freedom we may overlook the fact that the masses of us are to live by the productions of our hands, and fail to keep in mind that we shall prosper in proportion as we learn to dignify and glorify common labour and put brains and skill into the common occupations of life . . . . No race can prosper till it learns that there is as much dignity in tilling a field as in writing a poem. It is at the bottom of life we must begin, and not at the top.

passages.intro: Text 2 is from W. E. B. Du Bois's 1903 book The Souls of Black Folk.
passages.text: Mr. Washington represents in Negro thought the old attitude of adjustment and submission; but adjustment at such a peculiar time as to make his programme unique. This is an age of unusual economic development, and Mr. Washington's programme naturally takes an economic cast, becoming a gospel of Work and Money to such an extent as apparently almost completely to overshadow the higher aims of life.

items.stem: Based on the texts, how would Du Bois (Text 2) most likely respond to the list of fields in which Washington (Text 1) urges listeners to “cast down your bucket”?

choices.text: He would note that the list leaves out the political power and civil rights that Washington asks Black Americans to give up.
He would praise the list for including the professions, which require higher education.
He would argue that the list should have included agriculture and commerce.
He would agree that the list matches his own plan for the future of Black Americans.

items.explanation: Washington's list names agriculture, mechanics, commerce, domestic service, and the professions. Du Bois says Washington asks Black Americans to give up political power, civil rights, and higher education, none of which appear on the list.

rationales.B: The professions are on the list, but Du Bois says Washington asks people to give up higher education, so he would not praise the list on that ground.
rationales.C: Agriculture and commerce are already on Washington's list.
rationales.D: Du Bois describes Washington's policy critically, as a demand to give up rights, so he would not call it his own plan.

passages.intro: Text 1 is from a speech Booker T. Washington gave in Atlanta in 1895, printed in his 1901 autobiography Up from Slavery. He has just told a story about sailors who learned that the river water around their ship was fresh.
passages.text: To those of my race who depend on bettering their condition in a foreign land or who underestimate the importance of cultivating friendly relations with the Southern white man, who is their next-door neighbour, I would say: "Cast down your bucket where you are"—cast it down in making friends in every manly way of the people of all races by whom we are surrounded. Cast it down in agriculture, mechanics, in commerce, in domestic service, and in the professions.

passages.intro: Text 2 is from W. E. B. Du Bois's 1903 book The Souls of Black Folk.
passages.text: In answer to this, it has been claimed that the Negro can survive only through submission. Mr. Washington distinctly asks that black people give up, at least for the present, three things,— First, political power, Second, insistence on civil rights, Third, higher education of Negro youth,—and concentrate all their energies on industrial education, and accumulation of wealth, and the conciliation of the South.

items.stem: Based on the texts, Douglass (Text 1) and Washington (Text 2) would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.text: Each of them learned to read mainly with the help of a patient teacher.
Learning to read was a goal of great personal importance to each of them.
Each of them understood from early childhood why reading mattered so much.
Newspapers were the most valuable reading material for each of them.

items.explanation: Douglass calls his understanding of the “pathway from slavery to freedom” a grand achievement he “prized,” and Washington had “an intense longing to learn to read.” Both treat reading as deeply important.

rationales.A: Washington says he could find no one to teach him, so this does not fit Text 2.
rationales.C: Washington's longing began in early childhood, but Douglass describes his understanding as a sudden “new and special revelation.”
rationales.D: Only Washington mentions newspapers, and he lists them alongside common books.

passages.intro: Text 1 is from Frederick Douglass's 1845 autobiography. Douglass has just overheard his enslaver forbid anyone to teach him to read.
passages.text: These words sank deep into my heart, stirred up sentiments within that lay slumbering, and called into existence an entirely new train of thought. It was a new and special revelation, explaining dark and mysterious things, with which my youthful understanding had struggled, but struggled in vain. I now understood what had been to me a most perplexing difficulty—to wit, the white man's power to enslave the black man. It was a grand achievement, and I prized it highly. From that moment, I understood the pathway from slavery to freedom. It was just what I wanted, and I got it at a time when I the least expected it.

source.author: Frederick Douglass
source.title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave

passages.intro: Text 2 is from Booker T. Washington's 1901 autobiography Up from Slavery.
passages.text: From the time that I can remember having any thoughts about anything, I recall that I had an intense longing to learn to read. I determined, when quite a small child, that, if I accomplished nothing else in life, I would in some way get enough education to enable me to read common books and newspapers. . . . I had learned from somebody that the way to begin to read was to learn the alphabet, so I tried in all the ways I could think of to learn it,—all of course without a teacher, for I could find no one to teach me.

• In 1869, he spent a summer in the Sierra Nevada mountains of California.

• His account of that summer, My First Summer in the Sierra, was published in 1911.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize how long after the summer Muir's account of it was published. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.text: Muir, a naturalist who was born in Scotland, kept a journal during the summer of 1869.
My First Summer in the Sierra was published in 1911, three years before Muir's death.
Muir spent the summer of 1869 in the Sierra Nevada, but his account was not published until 1911.
In 1869, Muir spent a summer in the Sierra Nevada mountains of California and kept a journal.

items.explanation: To show how long the account waited, a sentence needs both dates: the summer of 1869 and publication in 1911. This choice gives both and marks the delay with “not published until.”

rationales.A: This mentions 1869 but not when the account was published.
rationales.B: This relates the publication to Muir's death, not to the summer the book describes.
rationales.D: This describes the summer but never says when the account appeared.

items.stem: The student wants to emphasize how early White recognized the importance of earthworms compared with Darwin. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.text: White wrote about the importance of earthworms in 1777, more than a century before Darwin's 1881 book.
Both White, in a letter, and Darwin, in a book, wrote about the effects that earthworms have on soil.
White, an English naturalist, lived most of his life in the village of Selborne.
Darwin's book about earthworms appeared in 1881, many years after White's death in 1793.

items.explanation: Comparing the two dates, 1777 and 1881, shows that White wrote about earthworms' importance more than a hundred years before Darwin's book.

rationales.B: This shows that both writers discussed earthworms but does not say which one wrote first or by how much.
rationales.C: This describes where White lived without mentioning earthworms or Darwin.
rationales.D: This compares Darwin's book with White's death rather than with White's writing about earthworms.

Bly circled the globe in 72 days, eight days faster than the journey in Verne's novel.
Jules Verne wrote a novel called Around the World in Eighty Days.
Bly's trip around the world began in 1889 and took 72 days.

• In 1823, she found the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaur, another marine reptile.

Mary and Joseph Anning found the skeleton of an ichthyosaur, a marine reptile, around 1811.
Both the ichthyosaur and the plesiosaur were marine reptiles.
In 1823, Mary Anning found the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaur.
