Charles Babbage designed a calculating machine called the Analytical Engine.
Lovelace added notes longer than the article itself, including a method for the engine to calculate Bernoulli numbers.
Ada Lovelace was an English mathematician who lived from 1815 to 1852.

items.explanation: The publication went beyond translation because of Lovelace's own additions. This choice describes those notes, their length, and their method for calculating Bernoulli numbers.

rationales.A: This describes only the translation, which is the part the goal says to go beyond.

rationales.D: This gives facts about Lovelace's life but not about her publication.

items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.text: Similarly,
For instance,
Nevertheless,
Consequently,

items.explanation: The first sentence suggests that shaking the ground brings worms out. The next sentence qualifies that: worms do not always come out. “Nevertheless” signals this contrast.

rationales.A: “Similarly” would introduce a matching point, but the second sentence limits the first instead of repeating it.
rationales.B: “For instance” would introduce an example of the peewit's trick working, but the sentence describes a case where it fails.
rationales.D: “Consequently” would present a result of the peewit's behavior, but worms staying put is not caused by it.

passage.intro: The following text is from Charles Darwin's 1881 book The Formation of Vegetable Mould, through the Action of Worms. Darwin is discussing what makes earthworms leave their burrows.
passage.text: The Peewit . . . seems to know instinctively that worms will emerge if the ground is made to tremble; for Bishop Stanley states (as I hear from Mr. Moorhouse) that a young peewit kept in confinement used to stand on one leg and beat the turf with the other leg until the worms crawled out of their burrows, when they were instantly devoured. Nevertheless, worms do not invariably leave their burrows when the ground is made to tremble, as I know by having beaten it with a spade, but perhaps it was beaten too violently.

source.author: Charles Darwin
source.title: The Formation of Vegetable Mould, through the Action of Worms

items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.text: For instance,
In contrast,
Nevertheless,
Consequently,

items.explanation: Darwin says many higher animals lack the worm's ability. Ants that keep trying to drag an object the hard way are an example of such an animal, so “For instance” fits.

rationales.B: Ants do differ from worms, but the sentence illustrates the claim about higher animals rather than setting up a new contrast.
rationales.C: “Nevertheless” would signal a point that goes against the claim, but the ants support it.
rationales.D: The ants' behavior is not a result of anything in the first sentence.

passage.intro: The following text is from Charles Darwin's 1881 book The Formation of Vegetable Mould, through the Action of Worms. Darwin has described how worms pull leaves into their burrows, trying different ways until one works.
passage.text: But it is surprising that an animal so low in the scale as a worm should have the capacity for acting in this manner, as many higher animals have no such capacity. For instance, ants may be seen vainly trying to drag an object transversely to their course, which could be easily drawn longitudinally . . .

items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.text: However,
For example,
Meanwhile,
Therefore,

items.explanation: Because the people's sense of time was not limited to one lifetime, it follows that they made plans lasting centuries. “Therefore” signals that result.

rationales.A: “However” signals a contrast, but long-range planning agrees with the time-sense just described.
rationales.B: Long-range planning is a consequence of the people's time-sense, not one example among several of it.
rationales.C: “Meanwhile” signals events happening at the same time, which does not fit a cause and its result.

passage.intro: The following text is from Charlotte Perkins Gilman's 1915 novel Herland. The narrator describes how the people of an isolated country think about their land.
passage.text: To them the country was a unit—it was theirs. They themselves were a unit, a conscious group; they thought in terms of the community. As such, their time-sense was not limited to the hopes and ambitions of an individual life. Therefore, they habitually considered and carried out plans for improvement which might cover centuries.

items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.text: However,
In fact,
As a result,
Similarly,

items.explanation: Washington first says he had no hat or cap. The next sentence goes further: he had never worn any covering on his head at all. “In fact” introduces this stronger version of the point.

rationales.A: “However” would signal a contrast, but the second sentence strengthens the first.
rationales.C: Never having worn a hat is not a result of noticing the other children's hats.
rationales.D: “Similarly” would introduce a separate, parallel point, but this sentence intensifies the same point.

passage.intro: The following text is from Booker T. Washington's 1901 autobiography Up from Slavery. He recalls his first days at school.
passage.text: When, however, I found myself at the school for the first time, I also found myself confronted with two other difficulties. In the first place, I found that all the other children wore hats or caps on their heads, and I had neither hat nor cap. In fact, I do not remember that up to the time of going to school I had ever worn any kind of covering upon my head, nor do I recall that either I or anybody else had even thought anything about the need of covering for my head.

items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.text: Instead,
For example,
In fact,
Meanwhile,

items.explanation: Washington says talking for its own sake never attracted him, then goes further: he considers such speaking “empty and unsatisfactory.” “In fact” introduces this stronger statement of the same view.

rationales.A: “Instead” would introduce an alternative, but the sentence restates and strengthens his dislike of empty speaking.
rationales.B: The sentence states his view more strongly; it does not give an example of anything.
rationales.D: “Meanwhile” signals something happening at the same time, which does not fit a restated opinion.

passage.intro: The following text is from Booker T. Washington's 1901 autobiography Up from Slavery. Miss Lord was one of his teachers.
passage.text: Whatever ability I may have as a public speaker I owe in a measure to Miss Lord. When she found out that I had some inclination in this direction, she gave me private lessons in the matter of breathing, emphasis, and articulation. Simply to be able to talk in public for the sake of talking has never had the least attraction to me. In fact, I consider that there is nothing so empty and unsatisfactory as mere abstract public speaking; but from my early childhood I have had a desire to do something to make the world better, and then to be able to speak to the world about that thing.

items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.text: Indeed,
Even so,
Otherwise,
By contrast,

items.explanation: The narrator says the people knew physiology well, then extends the point: in all the concrete sciences their results were surprising. “Indeed” introduces this stronger, broader claim.

rationales.B: “Even so” signals a result despite an obstacle, but nothing in the first sentence works against their skill.
rationales.C: “Otherwise” signals what would happen if something were not true, which does not fit two related claims.
rationales.D: Physiology is one of the concrete sciences the next sentence praises, so the sentence extends the point instead of contrasting with it.

passage.intro: The following text is from Charlotte Perkins Gilman's 1915 novel Herland. Three American men describe what they learned about the people of an isolated country.
passage.text: Physiology they were quite familiar with. Indeed, when it came to the simpler and more concrete sciences, wherein the subject matter was at hand and they had but to exercise their minds upon it, the results were surprising. They had worked out a chemistry, a botany, a physics, with all the blends where a science touches an art, or merges into an industry, to such fullness of knowledge as made us feel like schoolchildren.

items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.text: Therefore,
Nevertheless,
Similarly,
For example,

items.explanation: The text lists John's difficulties: divided families, careless parents, irregular children, and missing books. He kept going anyway, so “Nevertheless” signals that he struggled on despite them.

rationales.A: “Therefore” would make his hopeful struggle a result of the problems, but he continued in spite of them.
rationales.C: “Similarly” would add another problem, but the sentence turns to how John responded.
rationales.D: John's hopeful effort is not an example of the difficulties just listed.

passage.intro: The following text is from W. E. B. Du Bois's 1903 book The Souls of Black Folk. John has returned to his hometown in Georgia to open a school.
passage.text: For John, it had been a long, hard pull to get things started in the rickety old shanty that sheltered his school. The Negroes were rent into factions for and against him, the parents were careless, the children irregular and dirty, and books, pencils, and slates largely missing. Nevertheless, he struggled hopefully on, and seemed to see at last some glimmering of dawn. The attendance was larger and the children were a shade cleaner this week. Even the booby class in reading showed a little comforting progress. So John settled himself with renewed patience this afternoon.

items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.text: However,
Similarly,
In other words,
Therefore,

items.explanation: Thoreau states a principle, that people hit only what they aim at, and then draws a conclusion from it: they should aim at something high. “Therefore” signals that conclusion.

rationales.A: “However” signals a contrast, but aiming high follows from the principle instead of opposing it.
rationales.B: “Similarly” would add a parallel point, but the sentence draws a conclusion.
rationales.C: “In other words” would restate the principle, but the sentence gives advice based on it.

passage.intro: The following text is from Henry David Thoreau's 1854 book Walden.
passage.text: I cannot believe that our factory system is the best mode by which men may get clothing. The condition of the operatives is becoming every day more like that of the English; and it cannot be wondered at, since, as far as I have heard or observed, the principal object is, not that mankind may be well and honestly clad, but, unquestionably, that corporations may be enriched. In the long run men hit only what they aim at. Therefore, though they should fail immediately, they had better aim at something high.

items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.text: Still,
As a result,
For instance,
Likewise,

items.explanation: Anne says the history paper was hard and she got mixed up in the dates, yet she thinks she did fairly well. “Still” signals this outcome despite the difficulty.

rationales.B: Doing fairly well is not a result of getting mixed up in the dates; it happened in spite of that.
rationales.C: Her overall sense of the exam is not an example of getting the dates mixed up.
